extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and researchers in arithmetic geometry, anabelian geometry, and formalization (Lean) communities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating public claims about Inter-Universal Teichmüller theory (IUT), distinguishing responsible mathematical journalism from amateur/incorrect treatments, and criteria for pursuing Lean-style formalization of IUT. Focuses on standards of mathematical accountability, set-theoretic/universe issues, and practical steps for formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical accountability (EMSCOP Article 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians should make public claims of potential new theorems only when they believe they are able to provide full details in a timely manner, to avoid unnecessarily blocking an active line of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating 'blackholes' of accountability where validity becomes a matter of social/political dynamics rather than rigorous proofs; public assertions should be backed by precise statements and full proofs or timely plans to provide them; see discussion in §1.1 and references to the EMSCOP code of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer validation via peer-reviewed journals and seminars
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term digestion and rigorous examination of proofs should occur through internationally recognized mathematical journals with functional peer review systems and via lectures/workshops on the mathematics involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims made outside this infrastructural apparatus (e.g., by amateur journalism or non-peer-reviewed preprints) with skepticism until accountable mathematical details are available; see §1.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require professional mathematical training for substantive technical reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic or amateur reports on deep mathematics often lack the professional training necessary to evaluate technical claims reliably and can resemble LLM 'hallucinations'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing expository pieces, check the author's professional background, publication record in relevant areas, and whether they can provide precise technical details; cf. §1.2 discussion of Boyd and parallels to LLM output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ChatGPT-type 'hallucinations' and linguistic trickery
rubrics_metrics.description: Content produced without an accountability apparatus may be mere story-telling or mass-generated content divorced from mathematical reality (analogous to LLM hallucinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for opaque phrases or novel-sounding terminology used without rigorous definitions (example: misuse of 'arithmetic holomorphic structure'); demand explicit definitions and proofs rather than rhetorical flourishes (§1.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand precise statements and complete proofs for major claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Major claims (e.g., claims of logical relationships between simplified expositions and original IUT papers) must be supported by precise mathematical statements and complete proofs; absent these, the assertions are not established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Scholze–Stix manuscript is criticized for lacking a precise statement and proof of its central assertion; such absence is a valid reason to withhold acceptance of the claim (§1.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate interpretive/simplifying algorithms with logical equivalence to original theory
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation or simplification (algorithm) that reproduces some symbolic features does not automatically establish a logical relationship to the original theory unless one can show the connection precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholze–Stix's simplification/interpretation of a setup should not be taken as a logical refutation of IUT without rigorous linkage to IUT's formal statements (see SSA1/SSA2 discussion in §2.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence Principle for algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of an algorithm that is unsuccessful in yielding nontrivial consequences does not imply the non-existence of a different algorithm that does yield such consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this logical principle when judging attempts to disprove a theory by exhibiting an unsuccessful simplification or algorithm; explicitly discussed as (ExPr) in §2.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic labels distinguish elements/sets (not exotic 'universe-labeling')
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictions in IUT are not avoided by treating universes as essentially different in a novel way; instead, the relevant distinctions are ordinary set-theoretic labels for distinct elements/sets (e.g., vertices (n,m) of the oriented graph underlying the log-theta-lattice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'distinct universes' in IUT as arising from standard set-theoretic labeling conventions rather than as an unprecedented foundational trick; see LB1 and §2.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: No nontrivial set-theoretic structure is robust under arbitrary label-removals
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary identification (removal of distinct labels) of set-theoretic elements typically produces contradictions or destroys the relationship between structures; this is a general fact of set-theoretic mathematics, not a special vulnerability of IUT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple examples (e.g., identifying 2 and 3 in N producing contradictory arithmetic statements) to see that expecting robustness under arbitrary label-removal is misguided; see LB2 and Example 2.2.1 (§2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-universality phenomena are classical (compare SGA1 and homological algebra)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of universes/inter-universality in IUT is qualitatively the same at a foundational level as their use in classical contexts such as the profinite fundamental group (SGA1) or derived functors in homological algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that appearance of larger universes to obtain canonical constructions is classical and well-understood (DfUv1, DfUv2); do not treat inter-universality in IUT as unprecedented (§2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of larger universes for canonical constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical constructions (e.g., profinite fundamental groups, canonical cohomology modules) may require passing to a larger universe to avoid foundational contradictions tied to choices (basepoints, resolutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand why canonicality forces the use of universes and why eliminating universes by a naive 'identification' creates contradictions (violations of foundation); see the (DfUv1)/(DfUv2) discussion in §2.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean4 is, in principle, capable of formalizing IUT constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: At a theoretical level, formalization of Hodge-theaters, multiradial representations, and related IUT constructions in Lean4 presents no fundamental obstacles; Lean4 supports countably nested universes and has formalizations of comparable classical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical formalization will require substantial effort (years), choices about what to blackbox (assume), and large-scale coding work; see NoObs, LnCom, and §3.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean-formalization is immune to social/political stylistic issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing and executing Lean code does not require conforming to particular stylistic tastes or responding to social/political pressures about how a theory 'should' look; code forces explicit definitions and constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property makes Lean a neutral medium to settle certain formal questions, though coding choices themselves (e.g., whether to encode explicit labels) remain design decisions; see LnIm and §3.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary obstacle: shortage of people combining deep IUT knowledge and Lean expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The main practical obstacle to Lean-style formalization is the scarcity of professional mathematicians who both deeply understand IUT and are proficient at writing Lean code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addressing this requires training, collaboration between anabelian geometers and formalizers, and possibly reorganization of work (LnCom, ImApx in §3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization strategy: reorganize IUT into blackboxes and abstract combinatorial components
rubrics_metrics.description: To make IUT amenable to Lean formalization, reorganize the theory into blackboxes of classical anabelian/arithmetic geometry and isolate the remaining content as abstract formal/combinatorial arguments independent of heavy anabelian input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach (MthFm, BBxFm) reduces the burden on formalizers by isolating technical prerequisites; it is analogous to distilling essential logical structure (e.g., ∧(∨)-chain) in [EssLgc] (§3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean outputs could transform dissemination and evaluation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If Lean code becomes a practical and trusted medium for expressing mathematics, it could enable automated generation of expository materials and lead institutions to consider Lean artifacts in hiring/promotion/publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a forward-looking consideration (Asp3, Asp4): be mindful of possible cultural and institutional shifts if formalization becomes widespread (§3.1–§3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing fabricated, logically unrelated versions to satisfy tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformulations of IUT that are tailored to the tastes of different researchers, if not logically equivalent to the original theory, produce fabricated versions that create unnecessary confusion and mislead readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically check whether a reformulation preserves the logical content of IUT rather than merely producing an attractive but unrelated narrative; Scholze–Stix and other reformulations are cited as examples (§3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean can be used to verify falsification/confirmation of alleged contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal verification in Lean can establish (or refute) alleged logical contradictions in precise terms, so claims that Lean is 'fundamentally incapable' of resolving such disputes are unfounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lean to formalize concrete constructions (Hodge-theaters, algorithms) to validate or falsify supposed contradictions (response to FA1.3 and FA1.4 in §2.1 and §3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacrificing canonicality avoids universes but not indeterminacies
rubrics_metrics.description: One can avoid explicit use of universes by fixing small categories or small collections (sacrificing canonicality), but this does not remove substantive indeterminacies (e.g., inner automorphisms, homotopy equivalences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the trade-off: avoiding universes may simplify some formalization choices but preserves the essential inter-universality phenomena (SmCat, §2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute social/political consensus for mathematical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical truth should not be decided by social/political dynamics ('faith en masse'); rigorous proofs and verifiable constructions must be the basis for acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of appeals to consensus or rhetorical pressure; insist on formalizable arguments and peer-reviewed verification (discussion in §1 and (BlkAcc) references).
